text: Plan: 12 batches. Batch 1 is a broad survey of base feature families across lookbacks (returns/momentum, MA distance, vol, skew/kurt, beta/corr to panel, distance to rolling max/min). I also include probe pairs to learn harness semantics: cs_rank(ret(5)) vs ret(5) to see if cross-sectional ranking is applied automatically, and logret(5) vs ret(5). Direction is not a concern since neg() flips sign, so I focus on magnitude of SR first. Guiding principle against overfitting: prefer signal FAMILIES that work smoothly across adjacent lookbacks and survive simple robustness transforms, rather than single lucky parameterizations. Final top-3 should be economically distinct (e.g. reversal, vol/risk, trend) and ideally low-correlated with each other.

text: Findings so far. (1) Harness applies cross-sectional ranking automatically, so any monotone transform (cs_rank, cs_z, logret vs ret) is a no-op standalone, but cs_z is essential INSIDE add() to put components on a common scale. (2) The panel is reversal dominated at every horizon; neg(ret(250)) SR 1.22 is the single strongest raw signal, and the reversal family is smooth and monotone in lookback which argues it is real rather than a lucky parameter. (3) Vol normalization of the 250d reversal is a wash (1.19 to 1.26 across std lookbacks), which is reassuring: the edge is in the reversal itself, not in a tuned denominator. (4) kurt(20) SR 1.16 is a genuinely orthogonal second family; kurt peaks sharply at n=15 (1.58) which I treat as a parameter spike and hedge by blending kurt(15) with kurt(20). (5) Further weak but orthogonal components: vol contraction neg(div(std(5), std(60))), decorrelation neg(sub(corrm(20), corrm(250))), and neg(skew(120)). (6) beta(250) consistently RAISES IC (to 0.0120) but LOWERS Sharpe, so it adds cross-sectional information with volatile PnL; I exclude it since the objective is Sharpe. (7) Equal-weighted cs_z composites dominate: two-way reversal 1.61, four-way 2.06, six-way 2.38. Doubling any single component weight hurts, confirming equal weighting is the robust choice. Remaining plan: probe leftover feature space for one more orthogonal component, then stress-test the finalists for parameter sensitivity and pick three that share the robust diversified core but differ in details, so no single fragile parameter choice sinks all three out of sample.

text: Final selection logic. The winning architecture is an equal-weight cs_z composite of five economically distinct, low-correlation components: (1) long-horizon reversal neg(ret(250)), (2) short-horizon reversal neg(ret(5)), (3) short-window kurtosis, (4) decorrelation from the panel via a short-minus-long correlation spread, (5) negative skewness neg(skew(120)). Standalone these are only 0.5 to 1.7 SR; equal-weighted they reach 2.8, which is the signature of genuine diversification rather than a single overfit effect. Crucially, once the architecture is fixed the train SR is a plateau: over 40 distinct parameterizations land between 2.70 and 2.82. Differences at that level are noise, so I selected on robustness rather than on the train maximum. Two deliberate hedges: kurtosis peaks sharply at n=15 (1.58 vs 0.90 at n=10 and 1.16 at n=20), so I average cs_z of kurt(10), kurt(15) and kurt(20) rather than picking the peak; averaging costs nothing on train (blend 1.74 vs best single 1.72) while removing lookback-selection risk. Same for the decorrelation slot, where blending the corrm(10)-corrm(250) and corrm(10)-corrm(120) spreads holds 2.795. I rejected two tempting additions: beta(250) reliably raised IC to 0.0149 but LOWERED Sharpe every time it entered a composite, and blending ret(120) into the long-reversal slot hurt (2.66 vs 2.80), so ret(250) stays alone. I also verified equal weighting beats any doubling of a single component. A persistence check applying extra delay showed the composite decays quickly (SR 1.5 at delay 3, under 1.0 at delay 5), which is expected given two of the five components are fast-moving; the reported signals are scored at the standard 1-day lag. The three reported expressions share this validated core and differ only along the two axes carrying the most parameter risk, namely the kurtosis normalization (plain versus vol-adjusted) and whether the decorrelation slot is hedged, so no single fragile choice can sink all three out of sample.
